text: Welcome to Machine Learning Fundamentals, step five of the Data Scientist path. You already write Python, wrangle data in pandas, and reason with statistics. This course is where you learn how a computer can learn patterns from that data, and just as importantly, how to tell when it has learned something real. We start with the most basic question: what is machine learning?

In traditional programming, a person writes the rules — rules plus data go in, answers come out. Machine learning turns this around — you supply data together with the known answers, and an algorithm works out the rules itself. Those learned rules are the model. Imagine pricing houses: a rule-based approach might say under 1,200 square feet is $200k, under 2,200 is $320k, otherwise $450k — someone had to guess those thresholds, and every new market means rewriting them.

A machine-learning approach looks at past sales and finds the relationship itself. With 60 made-up houses whose price loosely follows their size, our hand-written rule predicts $320k for an 1,800 square foot house. The learned model, fit directly from the data, predicts $260.8k instead.

The learned model found a slope of about 0.119 thousand dollars per square foot, roughly $119, on a base of about $46,000. It recovered, from noisy examples, a pattern close to the one actually used to generate the data — 0.12 and 50. Nobody typed those numbers in. fit found them.

Some vocabulary you'll hear constantly: an example, sample, or row is one house, one customer, one order. Features, X, are the input columns the model can look at — here, size. The target or label, y, is the answer we want to predict — here, price. The model is the learned rules, stored as numbers inside a Python object. Training or fitting is learning those numbers from data; prediction or inference is using a fitted model on new rows.
Plotting the examples alongside the model's line shows exactly what learning meant here — the algorithm adjusted two numbers, the slope and the intercept, until the line sat close to the dots.

A model that memorizes the past is useless. What matters is how it performs on new data — houses that were not in the training set. This one idea drives almost everything in this course: how we split data, how we spot overfitting, how we choose between models.

Use machine learning when the pattern is too complicated or changes too often to write rules by hand, and you have plenty of past examples with answers. Don't use it when a clear rule already works, when you have almost no data, or when you can't tolerate any error. And remember — a model can only learn what's in its data; biased or messy data produces a biased or messy model.

To recap: machine learning means learning the rules from examples instead of writing them. Data with known answers goes in, a model comes out, and that model is judged on data it has never seen. Next up, lesson 2: supervised versus unsupervised learning.
